title: “An everlasting foundation” — the Greek has the righteous “turning aside” and being saved
summary: The KJV calls the righteous “an everlasting foundation”. Brenton’s Greek has no foundation: the righteous man, having turned aside (ἐκκλίνας), is saved for ever.
text: KJV Proverbs 10:25: “As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation.” Hebrew (WLC) 10:25: כַּעֲבֹ֣ור ס֭וּפָה וְאֵ֣ין רָשָׁ֑ע וְ֝צַדִּ֗יק יְסֹ֣וד עֹולָֽם׃. Brenton’s Greek 10:25: Παραπορευομένης καταιγίδος ἀφανίζεται ἀσεβὴς, δίκαιος δὲ ἐκκλίνας σώζεται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PRO10.htm) prints: “When the storm passes by, the ungodly vanishes away; but the righteous turns aside and escapes for ever.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/20/10/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PRO10.htm.
reasoning: The first half of the verse is a storm or whirlwind that passes and the wicked who are gone, and both texts say so. The second half differs. The KJV gives the righteous a place in a structure, a foundation that lasts. The Greek gives him an act (he turns aside) and a result (he is saved), with no foundation. A reader of each text takes a different picture of the righteous: something that stands under others, or someone who escapes.
scope: T applies to the second half of 10:25 only. Both texts agree on ‘for ever’ (עוֹלָם, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) and on the passing of the storm and the wicked. title: “A gift is as a precious stone” — the Greek has “instruction” as a gracious reward
summary: In the KJV a gift is like a precious stone in the eyes of the one who has it. In Brenton’s Greek the subject is παιδεία, which Brenton’s English renders “instruction”, and it is a gracious reward to those who use it.
text: KJV Proverbs 17:8: “A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth.” Hebrew (WLC) 17:8: אֶֽבֶן־חֵ֣ן הַ֭שֹּׁחַד בְּעֵינֵ֣י בְעָלָ֑יו אֶֽל־כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֖ר יִפְנֶ֣ה יַשְׂכִּֽיל׃. Brenton’s Greek 17:8: Μισθὸς χαρίτων παιδεία τοῖς χρωμένοις, οὗ δʼ ἂν ἐπιστρέψῃ εὐοδωθήσεται.. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PRO17.htm) prints: “Instruction is to them that use it a gracious reward: and whithersoever it may turn, it shall prosper.”. The second clause, that wherever it turns it prospers, stands in both.

title: “His neighbour findeth no favour in his eyes” — the Greek has the ungodly “not pitied by any man”
summary: The KJV says the soul of the wicked desires evil and his neighbour finds no favour in his eyes. Brenton’s Greek says only that the soul of the ungodly will not be pitied (οὐκ ἐλεηθήσεται) by any of mankind.

title: “Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind” — the Greek has “the north wind is sharp”
summary: The KJV of Proverbs 27:16 speaks of hiding a woman (from verse 15) as hiding the wind, and of ointment that betrays itself. Brenton’s Greek has Βορέας, the north wind, as a harsh wind that is nevertheless called by name ἐπιδέξιος, which Brenton’s English renders “propitious”.

title: “Bray a fool in a mortar” — the Greek has “scourge a fool … in the midst of the council”
summary: In the KJV a fool is brayed in a mortar among wheat with a pestle. In Brenton’s Greek the fool is scourged (μαστιγοῖς) and disgraced (ἀτιμάζων) in the midst of a council (συνεδρίου).
text: KJV Proverbs 27:22: “Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.” Hebrew (WLC) 27:22: אִ֥ם תִּכְתֹּֽושׁ־אֶת־הָאֱוִ֨יל ׀ בַּֽמַּכְתֵּ֡שׁ בְּתֹ֣וךְ הָ֭רִיפֹות בַּֽעֱלִ֑י לֹא־תָס֥וּר מֵ֝עָלָ֗יו אִוַּלְתֹּֽו׃ פ. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PRO27.htm) prints: “Though thou scourge a fool, disgracing him in the midst of the council, thou wilt still in no wise remove his folly from him.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/20/27/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PRO27.htm.
reasoning: The act in the KJV is crushing in a mortar with a pestle, among wheat. The act in the Greek is flogging with public shame before an assembly. They are different acts in different settings, though both end with the folly not leaving the fool.

title: “A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth” — the Greek says a bad man will not listen or say anything seasonable
summary: The KJV says a man has joy by the answer of his mouth and that a word in due season is good. Brenton’s Greek says the bad man (ὁ κακός) will not obey or attend to it, and will not say anything seasonable and good for the common good.
text: KJV Proverbs 15:23: “A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!” Hebrew (WLC) 15:23: שִׂמְחָ֣ה לָ֭אִישׁ בְּמַעֲנֵה־פִ֑יו וְדָבָ֖ר בְּעִתֹּ֣ו מַה־טֹּֽוב׃. Brenton’s Greek 15:23: Οὐ μὴ ὑπακούσει ὁ κακὸς αὐτῇ, οὐδὲ μὴ εἴπῃ καίριόν τι καὶ καλὸν τῷ κοινῷ.. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PRO15.htm) prints: “A bad man will by no means attend to counsel; neither will he say anything seasonable, or good for the common weal .”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/20/15/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PRO15.htm.
reasoning: The KJV verse is a statement of good: joy in a ready answer and the goodness of a timely word. The Greek verse is a statement about a bad man who does not do the good thing: no hearing and no seasonable word. The Greek keeps ‘seasonable’ (καίριον) and ‘good’ (καλόν), but turns them into things the bad man will not say. The person, the joy and the answer of his mouth are not in the Greek verse.

title: “A stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy” — the Greek has no fellowship with insolence
summary: In the KJV the heart knows its own bitterness and a stranger does not share its joy. In Brenton’s Greek a sensitive heart has a sorrowful soul, and when he rejoices he is not mixed with ὕβρις, which Brenton’s English renders “pride”.
text: KJV Proverbs 14:10: “The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.” Hebrew (WLC) 14:10: לֵ֗ב יֹ֭ודֵעַ מָרַּ֣ת נַפְשֹׁ֑ו וּ֝בְשִׂמְחָתֹ֗ו לֹא־יִתְעָ֥רַב זָֽר׃. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PRO14.htm) prints: “If a man's mind is intelligent, his soul is sorrowful; and when he rejoices, he has no fellowship with pride.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/20/14/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PRO14.htm.
reasoning: The KJV has a stranger (זָר) who is outside a person’s joy. The Greek has no stranger; the one who does not join the rejoicing is ὕβρις, insolence or pride. A stranger and pride are different things, so the two verses describe what is kept out of the joy differently.
